summary: Proposes On-Demand Mail Relay, a profile of SMTP that lets a site with a changing IP address collect its waiting mail by connecting to a provider. It is meant to be secure, extensible and easy to implement.

eli5.summary: A mailbox that waits for you to ring the bell before it hands over your mail, even if your home address changes each time.

questions: how to get email with a dynamic ip
subtitle: How a mail server with a changing IP address can call its provider and ask for the mail waiting for it.

tldr.problem: People running a mail server on an intermittent connection with a dynamic IP address have no widely deployed way to collect their queued mail, since ETRN only works for static addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The customer connects to the provider on port 366, authenticates with AUTH, and sends ATRN. The two sides then swap roles and the provider delivers the queued mail by ordinary SMTP.
tldr.outcome: A restricted profile of SMTP that is secure, extensible and easy to implement, proposed as a Standards Track protocol.

today: RFC 2645 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes ODMR as a restricted SMTP profile for customers with dynamic IP addresses.

sections.title: The Dynamic Address Problem
sections.content:
Low-cost systems and Internet connections have raised demand for local mail servers, often on a system that is connected to a service provider only some of the time. If such a system has a static IP address, the ESMTP ETRN command from RFC 1985 can be used to ask for queued mail. Systems with dynamic IP addresses, which are very common on low-cost connections, had no widely deployed solution.

RFC 2645 proposes On-Demand Mail Relay (ODMR) as a profile of SMTP that is secure, extensible and easy to implement.
sections.eli5: If your home keeps getting a different address, the post office cannot send mail to it on its own. So you have to call them and ask for your mail.

sections.title: How ODMR Works
sections.content:
ODMR is a restricted profile of SMTP, and port 366 is reserved for it. Because the roles reverse during the session, the RFC says customer and provider instead of client and server. The customer connects to the provider, authenticates and asks for its mail. The roles then reverse and normal SMTP proceeds.

The provider runs a process that listens on the ODMR port. It need not be a full SMTP server, but it must be an SMTP client with access to the outgoing mail queues and, as a server, implement EHLO, AUTH, ATRN and QUIT. Normally a mail transfer agent works through its queues on a timer or when new mail arrives. ODMR instead processes the queue on request. The provider keeps normal SMTP server duties, including delivery failure notices.
sections.eli5: The customer rings the provider's special doorbell, proves who they are, and asks for their mail. Then the two swap places so the provider can walk the mail over.

sections.title: The Three States
sections.content:
A session moves through an initial state, an authenticated state and a reversed state. In the initial state the provider is the server and three commands are valid: EHLO, AUTH and QUIT. The EHLO response MUST include AUTH and ATRN.

AUTH uses a SASL mechanism and the session is not authenticated until a success response is sent. For interoperability implementations MUST support CRAM-MD5. A site MAY disable it if it uses more secure methods, and other SASL mechanisms may be supported. The EXTERNAL mechanism might help when the provider has already authenticated the client, for example during a PPP connection.

In the authenticated state only ATRN and QUIT are valid. A provider MAY reject any other command with response code 502.
sections.eli5: There are three rooms. In the first you say hello and prove who you are. In the second you ask for your mail. In the third the provider hands it over.

sections.title: ATRN and the Reversal
sections.content:
ATRN (Authenticated TURN) differs from the old SMTP TURN command by optionally taking one or more domains. With no domains it means all domains the customer has access to. It MUST be rejected with 530 if the session is not authenticated, and its timeout MUST be at least 10 minutes so the provider can process its queue.

  • If the customer's authentication does not cover every listed domain, the provider MUST NOT send any mail and MUST reject with 450.
  • If access is fine but no mail is queued, the provider normally rejects with 453. It MAY instead reply 250 and send QUIT after reversing.
  • If mail exists in at least one domain, the provider replies 250.
  • If access cannot be checked, for example because a mapping database is unavailable, the reply is 451.
  • A 450 MAY also be used to refuse multiple requests within a time interval.

After the 250 reply the roles reverse. The customer sends a standard SMTP greeting, and the provider typically sends EHLO and then MAIL FROM and the rest of normal SMTP.
sections.eli5: Asking for your mail with a list of mailboxes only works if you are allowed to open all of them. If you are, and there is mail, the provider says yes and the two sides switch jobs.

sections.title: An Example Session
sections.content: The RFC's example uses example.net as the provider and example.org and example.com as customer domains. The customer authenticates with CRAM-MD5, sends ATRN example.org,example.com and gets 250 OK now reversing the connection. The customer then sends its own 220 greeting, the provider sends EHLO and the MAIL FROM and RCPT TO transfer follows, ending with QUIT from the provider.
sections.eli5: The customer says who they are and which mailboxes they want, the provider says okay, and then the provider delivers the letters one by one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ODMR is only useful with a prior arrangement, since the provider must be the target of MX records for the customer's domains and so hold mail to relay. The provider may therefore restrict access to the ODMR port, for example with a configurable server, a TCP wrapper or a firewall that blocks port 366 except inside the provider's network. This might suit a provider that is also the customer's ISP. It does not remove the need for AUTH but can add to its security.

Using SASL in AUTH allows more secure mechanisms to be substituted in the future.
sections.eli5: Only people with an arrangement with the provider can use the service, and the provider can also lock the doorbell so only certain visitors can reach it.
